stances.claim: The four Inquirer Filipino-of-the-Year RTC awardees -- Azucena, Palabrica, Soriano, Tamayo -- are deserving exemplars, but they are NOT exceptions; the great majority of trial judges are equally courageous, competent, and upright, and the public's negative generalization from a few scalawags is statistically unwarranted (under 200 of 2,000+ judges have complaints; under 20% of complaints are meritorious).
stances.rhetorical_move: exemplar-as-rule-not-exception reframing + statistical-rebuttal of negative generalization

stances.claim: Trial courts are the judicial frontliners closest to the great masses and where the vast majority of cases (~400,000 per year, less than 10% appealed) are resolved -- yet media disproportionately covers high-profile appellate and SC cases, distorting public perception of where justice actually lives.

Trial judges enjoy unique judicial prerogatives -- acquittals immediately final (except grave abuse), factual findings unreviewable in normal circumstances -- precisely BECAUSE they face the parties and witnesses directly in open court, whereas appellate justices work from cold records 'in the sanitized confines of their chambers.'
stances.rhetorical_move: prerogative-justified-by-proximity argument (the privilege follows from the burden)

stances.claim: The drug-case dominance (50% of 80% criminal load = ~40% of trial-court workload) makes mediation/compromise inapplicable to most RTC cases, structurally producing slower resolution -- meaning the 'Justice delayed is justice denied' lament has a structural cause beyond judicial diligence.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural-explanation for delay (not just management failure)

notable_anecdotes: The Inquirer's specific citation honoring the four judges for giving 'breath to the faltering idea that even those with neither wealth nor power can receive fair treatment in a court of law' -- preserved verbatim as the column's moral anchor.

The dramatic security contrast: trial judges 'dispersed to remote areas where they face serious security risks; in fact, many have been shot, injured and killed' -- versus appellate justices who are 'unreachable, secluded and faceless, deciding cases based largely on pleadings, memoranda and records elevated by the trial courts to the sanitized confines of their chambers.'

The statistical rebuttal of the scalawag generalization: 'less than 200 of the over 2,000 incumbent judges of both levels have pending complaints, and less than 20 percent of the complaints have been found meritorious' -- using ratios to flip the popular impression.
CJ's challenge to critics: 'Instead of just griping, those who disagree with the said data should lodge complaints against their perceived scalawags' -- translating gripe into procedural action.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban hails the Inquirer's Filipinos of the Year 2018 -- RTC Judges Rodolfo Azucena Jr., Arlene Lirag Palabrica, Andres Soriano, and Alexander Tamayo -- for giving 'breath to the faltering idea that even those with neither wealth nor power can receive fair treatment in a court of law,' and uses the citation as a springboard to defend trial judges generally as the judicial frontliners closest to the masses. He cites 2017 statistics -- 160,000 cases pending in 1,200 first-level courts and 640,000 in 1,100 RTCs with uneven distributions (some salas carrying 5,000 cases, others 50) -- and notes that 80% of cases are criminal (half drug-related and thus non-mediable), producing structural delay beyond judicial diligence. He observes that the vast majority of litigations end in trial courts (less than 10% of ~400,000 yearly resolutions are appealed, confirmed by appellate pending counts: CA 18,500, Sandiganbayan 5,500, CTA 1,200, SC 8,500). The four Inquirer awardees are deserving exemplars, he argues, but NOT exceptions: the great majority of trial judges are equally courageous, competent, and upright; the public's negative generalization from scalawags is statistically unwarranted, since fewer than 200 of the 2,000+ judges have pending complaints and fewer than 20% of those are meritorious. He stresses the contrast between trial judges -- dispersed to remote, often dangerous areas where many have been shot, injured, and killed, facing parties and witnesses directly in open court -- and appellate justices 'unreachable, secluded and faceless' in 'the sanitized confines of their chambers,' and explains that trial judges' unique prerogatives (acquittals immediately final, factual findings unreviewable in normal circumstances) follow from their proximity burden. He closes by hailing the unsung but equally courageous, competent, and upright trial judges who continue dispensing unheralded justice for the great masses.
